profile.reading:
This building is identified in mapping data as an Amazon Web Services facility near Donop Road on the south/west side of San Antonio, in Bexar County, Texas. DataCenterDynamics reported that AWS had filed plans to develop data centers in the San Antonio area, and the San Antonio Report has described Bexar County as home to at least 30 data centers from multiple operators, citing membership of Amazon, Microsoft, and Google in the industry group Data Center Coalition active in the region. Separately, local and trade coverage reported that Amazon Data Services Inc. filed Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation permits in March 2026 for three San Antonio-area data center projects: a roughly $65 million, 109,000 square foot building on the city's far West Side at 2200 Texas 211, on a 37.5-acre parcel Amazon had purchased in 2020; a 141,979 square foot building on the West Side; and a 119,407 square foot building on the Southeast Side. This research could not confirm with confidence which, if any, of those three specific TDLR filings corresponds to this exact registry entry near Donop Road, as opposed to a separate nearby Amazon project in the same metro area; the figures above describe Amazon's disclosed San Antonio activity generally rather than a confirmed specification for this building.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating that this research could confirm applies specifically to this mapped location, and no source found for this page breaks the San Antonio-area AWS footprint down building by building with certainty at this coordinate.

Amazon is widely reported in trade and business press to acquire and hold United States data center real estate through a subsidiary named Vadata, Inc., rather than directly under the Amazon.com or AWS names, a practice also seen with AWS campuses in Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, and elsewhere. This research did not pull a Bexar County Appraisal District or Tarrant Appraisal District parcel record to confirm Vadata, or another Amazon-linked entity, as the owner of the specific parcel at this coordinate; that county-level confirmation step, which the assignment for this page identifies as the most reliable source for hyperscaler-owned parcels with no public announcement, was not completed this pass and is noted here as follow-up work rather than assumed.

profile.regional_context: San Antonio and Bexar County, Texas have become an active data center market, with the San Antonio Report citing at least 30 facilities from multiple operators as of 2026, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google, CyrusOne, and Vantage Data Centers. CPS Energy, the city-owned utility, supplies power locally, and Bexar County and the City of San Antonio have negotiated economic development incentive agreements with several data center developers as the sector has grown, a trend covered by the San Antonio Report and regional business press. Texas as a whole has drawn large hyperscale data center investment in recent years, including AWS filings for other campuses near Houston, reported by DataCenterDynamics.

reading.body:
AWS operates this facility in Bexar County on the south side of San Antonio, but does not publish specific power capacity, square footage, or technical specifications for individual data center buildings as a matter of company policy. Local reporting suggests an approximately $65 million AWS data center project on San Antonio's south side, though this research could not confirm whether that figure corresponds to this specific facility or a separate nearby AWS development.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities of which 18 publish power capacity figures totaling 468 MW. This facility is ranked 19th by published capacity in the state, which means it does not appear in the published figure set, consistent with AWS's nondisclosure of per-building specifications.

Without published capacity data, the facility's significance to AI infrastructure scaling cannot be assessed from operator disclosures. The location places it in San Antonio's growing data center corridor, part of a larger regional development in Texas that now hosts dozens of operators, but its contribution to grid demand and AI compute availability remains unknown outside AWS's internal planning.
